messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 74
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Physical Therapist
- Trauma Type: Refugee
- Pcl5: 35

# Marta

Marta is a 74-year-old woman who has spent the better part of five decades helping other people move through pain. As a physical therapist, she has always understood the body's capacity to carry what the mind cannot easily name. She knows about muscle memory, about the way tension lodges itself in tissue long after the original injury has healed. What she did not fully reckon with, until recently, is how thoroughly that principle applies to her own life.

She was eleven years old when her family left Hungary in the winter of 1956, in the weeks following the Soviet crackdown on the uprising. She remembers the cold most of all — a particular, merciless cold that came up through the ground as the family moved on foot through fields at the edge of the Austrian border. Her father carried her younger brother. Her mother held her hand so tightly that Marta's fingers went numb, and she was not sure for a long time whether it was the frost or the grip. There were other people moving alongside them in the dark, strangers who had become temporary family by necessity. At one point, there were shouts somewhere behind them, and everyone dropped to the ground without a word, faces pressed into the frozen earth, and Marta understood without being told that making a sound might mean they would not survive the night.

They did survive. They made it to Vienna, and eventually to England, and Marta built a life that by most measures has been full and fortunate. She married a kind man named Geoffrey, raised two children, and found genuine meaning in her work. For decades, the memories of that night existed as a kind of sealed room inside her — present, but not entered.

Then, two winters ago, her granddaughter showed her a news broadcast. Families at a European border, night footage, people moving through cold and darkness with children in their arms. Marta watched for perhaps forty seconds before she had to leave the room. She told Geoffrey she felt unwell, which was true, though not in any way she could immediately explain. That night she did not sleep. She lay in the dark and felt the cold from 1956 in her hands, felt the grip of her mother's fingers, heard sounds that were not in the room.

Since then, the sealed room has been open. She finds herself startled by things that should not startle her — a door closing firmly, a car backfiring in the street outside the clinic. She notices that she scans exits when she enters unfamiliar spaces, something she has apparently always done but only recently begun to observe in herself. She dreams of the border crossing several times a week, and in the dreams she is always eleven, always cold, and the shouts behind her are always getting closer.

At work, she remains competent and present with her patients — that part of her, she says, has always felt safe. But she finds it harder to concentrate on documentation afterward, and she sometimes sits in her car in the car park for longer than she intends, not quite ready to re-enter the world. She has told Geoffrey some of this, and he listens with the patience she has always loved in him, but she can see that he does not entirely know what to do with it, and she does not entirely blame him.

What troubles her most, she says quietly, is the shame attached to it. She is seventy-four years old. She has a profession built on understanding how the body heals. She has had, she insists, a good life. She cannot quite account for why a television broadcast should undo something she believed she had long since resolved. She speaks about the eleven-year-old girl in the field with a kind of careful distance, as though she is describing someone she once knew but lost track of — and perhaps that is, in some sense, exactly what happened.
